# Closing: a world that shrank unevenly {.unnumbered}

It is tempting to tell this story as one smooth acceleration. The maps say otherwise.

The shrinking was uneven in time. For more than fifteen centuries travel barely changed, and in some ways it went backwards: a Roman in Lutetia could reach Rome faster than a Parisian in 1300. Then, in less than a century, from the turgotine coaches of the 1770s to the steamships and railways of the 1850s, the old limits fell one after another.

It was uneven in space. Every map in this book shows fast corridors and slow gaps: the Rhône and the sea lanes for the Romans, the post roads for the diligence, the first railway spokes around Paris in 1850, the air routes of 1950. Being near a line mattered more than being near Paris.

It was uneven between people. The fastest journey was almost always a privilege: the state post of Rome, the first-class-only Orient Express, the Collins liners with no steerage, Concorde's hundred seats. Most travellers, from the Bordeaux Pilgrim to the emigrants of Le Havre, moved at the slower pace below the headline figures. Only in the last half century has fast travel become ordinary.

It was uneven in permission. The medieval traveller relied on a letter from someone powerful, and the nineteenth-century traveller on a passport *visé* at every frontier. On the eve of the First World War most of Europe asked for no papers at all, until the war brought the passport back for good. Much of Europe has since dropped its internal border checks again, while a journey beyond it often begins with an online authorization.

And from 1794, the story split in two. News began to outrun people with Chappe's telegraph and crossed the oceans with the cable of 1866. Since then the maps in this book describe the movement of people; news has travelled on its own, almost instantly.

The last chapter adds a final twist. Since the 1970s, long-distance travel times have stopped falling. The world did not keep shrinking; it filled up instead, with nearly five billion passenger journeys by air a year.
